summary: Discusses SMTP operational experience in mixed IPv4 and IPv6 dual stack environments. It explains problems seen with MX record configurations for stable dual-stack mail delivery and defines operational requirements for it.

eli5.summary: When a town has both old and new street numbering, mail can get lost unless the post office's directory is set up carefully. This memo says how.

questions: mx records for both ipv4 and ipv6
subtitle: Keeping mail flowing when DNS has both old and new address formats.

tldr.problem: As organizations transition from IPv4 to IPv6, mail servers configured for only one protocol fail to reach recipients on the other, breaking email delivery unless DNS and SMTP sender behavior are carefully coordinated.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC clarifies how SMTP senders should look up both A records (IPv4 addresses) and AAAA records (IPv6 addresses) for MX targets, and specifies MX configurations that ensure both IPv4 and IPv6 senders can reach a domain's mail servers.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can operate stable dual-stack email during the IPv4-to-IPv6 transition by ensuring MX targets have both address types and that primary mail servers support both protocols.

facts.label: Preference order
facts.value: AAAA records prioritized over A records

today: RFC 3974 is Informational and describes experiences from the IPv4-to-IPv6 transition period (early 2000s). Most modern SMTP implementations now support IPv6, though dual-stack email remains the safest configuration during continued coexistence.

sections.title: The Dual-Stack Email Problem
sections.content:
SMTP mail delivery relies on DNS: senders look up MX records to find the mail server for a domain, then look up A records (for IPv4) or AAAA records (for IPv6) to find the server's IP address. In a transition period where some organizations are IPv4-only and others are IPv6-capable, mail can fail to deliver if the directory is misconfigured.

An organization with an IPv6-only mail server will not receive mail from IPv4-only senders. Similarly, an IPv4-only server will not reach IPv6-only senders. This document clarifies the problems and defines operational requirements to keep mail flowing during the transition.
sections.eli5: Some post offices only know IPv4 addresses, and some only know IPv6. If a mail server only has one type of address in the directory, the other kind of sender will get lost.

sections.title: MX Records and Address Records
sections.content:
MX records point to mail servers by name. When a sender looks up an MX record like 'mx1.example.org,' it then queries DNS for that name's addresses. During the transition, both A records (IPv4) and AAAA records (IPv6) should be present for the same name.

For example, a domain might define MX records pointing to 'mx1.example.org' (dual-stack with both A and AAAA), and 'mx10.example.org' (IPv6-only with only AAAA). This works if senders try both address families, but requires careful coordination among MX targets to ensure mail doesn't get stuck on a secondary server that cannot reach the primary.
sections.eli5: The directory entry for each mail server should list both its IPv4 address and its IPv6 address, like giving both an old and new street number.

sections.title: SMTP Sender Algorithm in Dual-Stack
sections.content:
A dual-stack SMTP sender should follow this algorithm: (1) look up MX records for the destination, (2) skip lower-preference MX records if the sender's own name appears, (3) for each MX target, look up A records if the sender supports IPv4, (4) look up AAAA records if the sender supports IPv6, (5) if no addresses are found, skip to the next MX record, (6) attempt a TCP connection to each address in sequence, preferring AAAA (IPv6) records over A records to encourage the transition.

The RFC recommends that AAAA lookups should be done independently if DNS does not return them in the additional section. If all addresses fail, try the next MX record. Only after exhausting all MX records should the sender report a temporary failure.
sections.eli5: When sending mail, try IPv6 first, then IPv4. If one mail server doesn't work, try the next one on the list. Keep trying addresses until mail goes through.

sections.title: Configuring MX for Reachability
sections.content:
For stable dual-stack operation, the RFC recommends that the primary MX host be configured as dual-stack (supporting both IPv4 and IPv6). This ensures secondary MX servers can relay mail to the primary regardless of their own protocol support.

If the primary MX is IPv6-only and secondary MX servers are IPv4-only, a secondary server that receives mail cannot forward it to the primary, causing mail to accumulate on the secondary. Alternatively, organizations can use other mechanisms like shared storage (NFS) or protocol translators to work around protocol mismatches, but dual-stack primary MX is the simplest approach.
sections.eli5: The main mail server should speak both IPv4 and IPv6. That way, backup servers can always talk to it, no matter which protocol they use.

sections.title: Lessons Learned
sections.content:
The RFC documents operational experience showing that most IPv6-ready MTAs implement the algorithm correctly. However, problems have been observed with misconfigured DNS servers that return SERVFAIL (temporary error) on AAAA queries, causing mail to be queued unnecessarily. When a broken DNS server causes such delays, fixing the DNS server is the remedy.

The RFC also notes that the SMTP protocol revision (RFC 2821) should be updated to explicitly document IPv6 concerns and the ordering preference between A and AAAA records for all implementations to follow consistently.
sections.eli5: Most mail systems work fine with both IPv4 and IPv6. Broken DNS servers sometimes cause problems, and they should be fixed.
